_comment: Static agronomic reference text keyed by the dataset's raw class name. This is reference material shown next to a prediction - it is never used to produce or influence a prediction. Sources: PlantVillage class definitions and standard extension-service descriptions.

_fallback.description: This condition is part of the trained class list but no reference description has been added yet.

Tomato___healthy.description: No disease symptoms detected. The leaf shows uniform green pigmentation with intact margins and no lesions.
symptoms: Uniform green colour
No necrotic spots or lesions
Intact leaf margins
management: Continue the current irrigation and nutrition schedule
Keep scouting weekly, especially the lower canopy
Maintain airflow between plants to limit leaf wetness

Tomato___Early_blight.description: Early blight is caused by the fungus Alternaria solani. It starts on older, lower leaves and progresses upward, reducing photosynthetic area and causing premature defoliation.
symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric rings, giving a target-board pattern
Yellow halo surrounding each lesion
Lower, older leaves affected first
Progressive defoliation from the base upward
management: Remove and destroy affected lower leaves
Apply a protectant fungicide such as chlorothalonil or mancozeb on the recommended interval
Mulch the soil surface to stop rain-splash of spores
Rotate away from solanaceous crops for two to three seasons

Tomato___Late_blight.description: Late blight is caused by the oomycete Phytophthora infestans. It spreads extremely fast in cool, wet weather and can destroy an entire field within days, which makes it the most urgent condition in this class list.
symptoms: Large, irregular, water-soaked greasy grey-green patches
White fuzzy sporulation on the underside of the leaf in humid conditions
Rapidly spreading brown-black lesions without a distinct ring pattern
Firm brown rot on fruit
management: Act immediately - remove and destroy infected plants away from the field
Apply a systemic fungicide containing metalaxyl or cymoxanil
Avoid overhead irrigation and evening watering
Plant certified disease-free seed and resistant cultivars

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.description: Leaf mould, caused by Passalora fulva (formerly Cladosporium fulvum), is primarily a greenhouse and polyhouse disease driven by sustained high humidity.
symptoms: Pale green to yellow diffuse patches on the upper leaf surface
Olive-green to grey-brown velvety mould on the lower surface
Leaves curl, wither and drop while remaining attached for a while
Rarely affects fruit directly
management: Reduce humidity below 85 percent through ventilation and spacing
Avoid wetting the foliage when irrigating
Apply chlorothalonil or a copper-based fungicide
Remove crop debris at the end of the season

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.description: Septoria leaf spot is caused by the fungus Septoria lycopersici. It overwinters in crop debris and is spread by rain splash and overhead irrigation.
symptoms: Many small circular spots, 1 to 3 mm, with grey centres and dark brown borders
Tiny black fruiting bodies visible inside the spot centres
Starts on the lowest leaves after fruit set
Heavy defoliation in severe cases
management: Remove infected lower foliage promptly
Switch to drip irrigation to keep leaves dry
Apply mancozeb or a copper fungicide at 7 to 10 day intervals
Clear and destroy all crop residue after harvest

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot is caused by several Xanthomonas species. It is seed-borne and worsens with warm, wet, windy weather.
symptoms: Small dark water-soaked spots that turn brown and angular
Spots often surrounded by a yellow margin
Scabby raised lesions on fruit
Leaf margins become ragged and torn
management: Use certified pathogen-free seed and transplants
Apply copper-based bactericides, often tank-mixed with mancozeb
Avoid working in the field while the foliage is wet
Rotate crops and remove volunteer solanaceous plants

Tomato___Target_Spot.description: Target spot is caused by Corynespora cassiicola and affects leaves, stems and fruit, often confused with early blight.
symptoms: Small brown spots that enlarge into lesions with concentric rings
Light tan centres that may crack
Pitted sunken lesions on fruit
management: Improve canopy airflow by pruning and correct spacing
Apply a fungicide programme rotating active ingredients
Remove infected debris from the field

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.description: Damage caused by the two-spotted spider mite (Tetranychus urticae), a sap-sucking pest rather than a pathogen. It thrives in hot, dry, dusty conditions.
symptoms: Fine pale stippling or speckling across the leaf surface
Bronze or rusty discolouration as damage accumulates
Fine webbing on the leaf underside
Leaves dry out and drop
management: Spray a miticide or horticultural oil, covering the leaf underside
Raise humidity and wash down foliage to suppress populations
Introduce predatory mites such as Phytoseiulus persimilis
Control dust along field edges and roads

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.description: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus (TYLCV) is a begomovirus transmitted by the whitefly Bemisia tabaci. There is no curative treatment once a plant is infected.
symptoms: Severe upward curling and cupping of leaves
Marked yellowing of leaf margins
Stunted growth with shortened internodes
Flower drop and heavy yield loss
management: Remove and destroy infected plants to cut the inoculum source
Control whiteflies with yellow sticky traps and approved insecticides
Use insect-proof nets in the nursery stage
Plant TYLCV-resistant varieties

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.description: Tomato mosaic virus (ToMV) is a highly stable virus spread mechanically by hands, tools and contaminated seed.
symptoms: Light and dark green mottled mosaic pattern
Fern-like narrowing or distortion of young leaves
Stunted plants with uneven ripening
Internal browning of fruit
management: Remove infected plants and wash hands and tools with disinfectant
Do not smoke or handle tobacco near the crop
Use certified virus-free seed and resistant cultivars
Avoid unnecessary handling of the foliage

Potato___healthy.description: No disease symptoms detected. The compound leaf shows healthy green tissue with no lesions or chlorosis.
symptoms: Uniform green foliage
No lesions or wilting
Normal leaflet shape
management: Maintain balanced fertigation
Scout weekly for early blight on lower leaves
Keep hilling adequate to protect tubers

Potato___Early_blight.description: Potato early blight, caused by Alternaria solani, builds up through the season and is worst on nitrogen-deficient or stressed plants.
symptoms: Dark brown lesions with concentric target-like rings
Lesions bounded by leaf veins, giving an angular outline
Yellowing around the lesions
Oldest leaves affected first
management: Apply a protectant fungicide such as mancozeb or chlorothalonil
Keep nitrogen nutrition adequate to delay leaf senescence
Rotate out of potato and tomato for at least two seasons
Destroy cull piles and volunteer plants

Potato___Late_blight.description: Potato late blight, caused by Phytophthora infestans, is the disease responsible for historic famine-scale crop losses. It can destroy a field in under a week under cool wet conditions.
symptoms: Water-soaked pale green patches that turn brown-black
White sporulating ring at the lesion edge on the leaf underside
Blackened petioles and stems
Reddish-brown granular tuber rot
management: Treat as urgent - destroy infected foliage immediately
Apply a systemic fungicide such as metalaxyl or dimethomorph
Plant certified seed tubers and resistant varieties
Destroy the haulm before harvest to protect tubers

Pepper,_bell___healthy.description: No disease symptoms detected. The leaf shows glossy uniform green tissue with no spots or deformation.
symptoms: Glossy uniform green colour
No necrotic spots
Normal leaf shape
management: Maintain consistent soil moisture
Scout for aphids and whiteflies on the leaf underside
Avoid overhead irrigation late in the day

Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot of pepper is caused by Xanthomonas species. It is seed-borne, spreads in warm wet weather and can defoliate plants enough to cause fruit sunscald.
symptoms: Small water-soaked spots that become brown and necrotic
Angular lesions limited by the leaf veins
Yellowing and premature leaf drop
Raised rough scabby spots on fruit
management: Use certified pathogen-free seed; hot-water treat suspect seed
Spray copper plus mancozeb preventively
Never cultivate or harvest while the foliage is wet
Rotate for at least one year and remove crop debris
